p3_b4.ocr: Thicknesses of the subfoveal CS layer and the large vessel layer Subfoveal CS layer thickness by age. Mean CS layer thickness values (±SD) for each age decade were; 20s: 110.78±40.80 μm, 30s: 89.89±25.16 μm, 40s: 73.11±28.25 μm, 50s: 54.56 ±23.03 μm, 60s: 50.57±29.06 μm, 70s: 55.42±38.37 μm, and 80s: 39.89±32.47 μm. There was a linear relationship between CS layer thickness and age (Fig 4). The regression formula is: CS layer thickness (μm) = 125.71–1.08×age (p<0.0001, R2 = 0.29). Subfoveal choroidal large vessel layer thickness by age. Mean subfoveal choroidal thick- ness values (±SD) of the large vessel layer for each age decade were; 20s: 214.56±74.54 μm, 30s: 239.5±88.86 μm, 40s: 225.59±47.75 μm, 50s: 183.40±55.08 μm, 60s: 185.86±58.76 μm, 70s: 189.26±49.82 μm, and 80s: 200.00±48.53 μm. There was a linear relationship between large vessel layer thickness and age (Fig 5). The regression formula is: choroidal large vessel layer thickness (μm) = 250.07–0.87×age (p<0.0209, R2 = 0.056). A significant age-dependent difference in choroidal thickness was observed for both the CS layer (p<0.0001) and the large vessel layer (p<0.0209) (Table 7, Figs 4 and 5). The statistical power was 0.493, which was calculated based on a previous report, employing a distance of ‘23 μm’ for our 68 subjects (significance level of 0.05).[14] Discussion Chen et al reported axial length to be the main predictor of foveal choroidal thickness but they did not examine refractive error [17].
